title: What's the deal with duckbill platypuses?
summary: Josh and Chuck cover the duckbill platypus: its small size and freshwater habitat in eastern Australia and Tasmania, early European disbelief and the 1802 confirmation by Everard Home (transcribed as "Everard Jones"), its mammal traits (milk through the abdomen, puggles), egg-laying, monotreme status, electroreception through bill pores, venom from males' hind-foot spurs, and the 2008 Platypus Genome Project with its unusual sex chromosomes. The episode closes with a listener mail from Penelope about the Red Cross blood donation ban on men who have sex with men and a call for more inclusive wording when discussing blood donation.

segments.title: Opening banter and zoological edition
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the zoological episode topic and joke about the platypus being a new subject for the show, with a 'spoiler free' tease about its venom.

segments.title: Size, habitat and diving
segments.summary: The hosts note that platypuses are much smaller than expected, about five pounds with southern animals larger and northern ones around two and a half to three pounds. They live in freshwater rivers and streams in eastern Australia and Tasmania, and feed as bottom feeders while holding their breath, with conflicting estimates of how long they can stay underwater.

segments.title: Gondwana origins and early European discovery
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the platypus's presence in eastern Australia and its ancestry tied to the breakup of Gondwana. They describe Aboriginal names for the animal, then the 19th-century European encounters, skepticism that treated specimens as fakes like the Chinese mermaid mummies, and the 1802 dissection by Everard Home that confirmed it was real.

segments.title: Mammal traits, puggles, and egg-laying
segments.summary: The hosts explain that the platypus is a mammal because females produce milk secreted through the abdomen, with no nipples, and young puggles suckle from it. They also note it lays one to three leathery eggs, has reptile-like eyes and bird-like features, and that its young are born with teeth that fall out, which lets creationists and evolutionists each claim it as evidence.

segments.title: Monotremes and electroreception
segments.summary: The hosts describe the platypus as one of two monotremes, the group whose members share one cloacal opening for excretion and reproduction, alongside the spiny anteater. They then cover how platypuses find food with electroreceptors in the bill pores while their eyes and nostrils are closed underwater, and how they store food in their cheeks and grind it with gravel.

segments.title: Venom and the spur
segments.summary: The hosts discuss that the platypus is one of only three mammal types that produce venom, mentioning the spiny anteater and certain shrews and solenodons. Males have a venomous spur on the hind foot used mainly in spring, likely for fighting other males. Venom can hurt humans badly with no known pain treatment, and has harmed dogs.

segments.title: Platypus Genome Project and sex chromosomes
segments.summary: The hosts describe the Platypus Genome Project started in 2008 by about a hundred scientists. Findings include ten sex chromosomes instead of two, some genes shared with birds' Z chromosome, and a venom composition similar to reptile venom but evolved independently. The hosts discuss implications for understanding human evolution and possible links to ovarian cancer.

segments.title: Closing remarks on the platypus
segments.summary: The hosts wrap up the platypus discussion, calling it a hodgepodge animal, and mention the How Stuff Works article and Animal Planet resources for further reading.

segments.title: Listener mail: Red Cross blood donation policy
segments.summary: Listener Penelope writes that the Red Cross bans men who have sex with men from donating blood indefinitely and requires a one-year wait for women who have sex with men, and urges the hosts to word blood-donation advice to include only those who are allowed to give. Josh and Chuck agree and thank her, then give social media and email contact info.
